sentences.text: As a result of the accident, petitioner sustained grievous injuries and he was taken to Deepak Memorial Hospital, Delhi, where his treatment was conducted.

During investigation, it was found that at the time of accident, the offending vehicle was not insured and it was being driven by respondent no.1 and owned by respondent no.2.

sentences.text: It is settled law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non
. However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v.
Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand &
Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018, Law Suit (SC) 303.

He specifically mentioned that a green coloured box was affixed on the offending vehicle bearing the name 'Hari Mirch Masala Restaurant' and he also noted the registration number of the offending vehicle as DL7SBZ-7623.

10. Per contra, R2W1 Vinay Kumar, owner of the offending vehicle deposed that no accident had taken place with the alleged offending vehicle as it was subsequently seized by the police and falsely i m p l i c a t e d

sentences.text: He stated that on the date of alleged accident i.e. on 30.01.2017, it was Monday and on Monday, the vehicle was lying at shop due to weekly Monday bazaar and heavy rush on road.

I may note that though during cross-examination, the witness stated that on 30.01.2017 (Monday), he did not send Shobi Lal (respondent no.1) for delivery and that due to Monday Market rush, they do not send their bikes for delivery, however, at the same time, he admitted that their restaurant is opened on Monday and that they clean their restaurant on Monday and also serve food.

Thus, in this scenario,
statemnet of R2W1 does not inspire confidence on the plea that he had not sent the respondent no.1 for delivery on the day of alleged accident.

Furthermore, the plea of false implication of the offending vehicle is also not sustainable in my considered view because no corroborative evidence in support of said contention has been placed on record by R2W1 i.e. the complaint to senior police officers or higher authorities regarding false implication or any previous enmity.

sentences.text: Moreover, it has been argued by learned counsel for the respondents that the alleged accident is stated to have occurred on 30.01.2017, whereas, the FIR was lodged on 16.02.2017, which indicates that the FIR is an afterthought step to falsely implicate the alleged offending vehicle.
On this, I may note that the explanation of delay in lodging the FIR has already been furnished by the petitioner in the FIR itself which was lodged on 16.02.2017 on his statement.

Perusal of FIR shows that the petitioner stated therein that after the accident, he had called his son on the spot and his son let the driver/ respondent no.1 go from there and he removed him (petitioner) to Deepak Memorial Hospital, where due to severe pain and with a view to get the instant treatment, he told the ________________________________________________________________________________ MACT no. 350/2017; Sharad Kishore Srivastava v. sentences.text: In his testimony also, PW1 petitioner affirmed this fact that he had not told the doctor about the accident.

MLC of the petitioner, which he got prepared subsequently on 16.02.2017, also shows the endorsement made thereon by the petitioner mentioning the fact that, in actual, he had sustained injuries as a result of the accident.

12. Furthermore, in the FIR as well as in his testimony, the petitioner (PW1) categorically stated the registration number of the offending vehicle while giving its specific description that a green colour box was affixed on it showing the name 'Hari Mirch Masala Restaurant'.

On perusal of the Mechanical Inspection Report, which is part of the DAR (Ex.PW1/1), I may note that delivery box fitted at back seat (green colour) was found scratched, which corroborates the version of the petitioner.

Besides, the offending vehicle was found to have sustained other fresh accidental damages (front number plate damaged; front head light/ side indicator scratched; handle bar pressed/ left mirror damaged; lever (muththa) scratched; left side leg guard scratched, etc.), which are sufficient to strengthen the version of the petitioner that the offending vehicle was involved in the accident.

Furthermore, the version of the petitioner that while he was crossing the road in front of Vidyut Apartment, the offending vehicle came from the side of Mother Dairy/ Gurudwara, Madhu Vihar and hit him finds strength from the Site Plan, which is also part of the DAR Ex.PW1/1 (colly).
Also, in the cross-examination of PW1, I found no such contradiction or inconsistency which could create any doubt upon the veracity of his testimony.

Whether the petitioner is entitled for any compensation, if so, to what amount and f r o m

sentences.text: In view of the finding on Issue no.1, petitioner is entitled to get the compensation,

however,
quantum of compensation still needs to be adjudicated.
Section 168 of M.V. Act, 1988 enjoins upon the claim Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation, which appears to be just and reasonable.

As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v.
Willoughby (1970) AC 467, page 492 per Lord Reid).

17. The present claim petition pertains to injury and scope of compensation in injury cases has been considered by Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Mr. R.D. Hattangadi v. M/S Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755.

entities.text: R.D. Hattangadi v. M/S Pest Control (India) Pvt. Ltd., 1995 AIR 755
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant extract is as under:
"Broadly speaking while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages.

Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which is capable of being calculated in terms of money-, whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations.

In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may, include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit upto the date of trial; (iii) other material loss.
So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned

,
they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit;

inconvenience, discomfort, disappointment, hardship, frustration and mental stress in life."

sentences.text: 18. Further, in Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India laid down general principles for computation of compensation in injury cases.

entities.text: Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar & another (2011) 1 SCC 343
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant paras of the judgment are reproduced as under:
5.

The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

6. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary Damages (special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food and miscellaneous expenditure.

(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
________________________________________________________________________________ MACT no. 350/2017; Sharad Kishore Srivastava v. Shobi Lal & Ors.; 9 of 13 Pages (a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment.
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses.
Non-Pecuniary Damages (general damages)
(iv) Damages to pain, suffering and trauma as a consequence of the injuries.

sentences.text: (v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage)
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (I), (ii), (a) and (iv).

It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii), (b), (iii), (v)
and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
19.
In the instant case, the petitioner did not seek reimbursement of the medical expenses incurred in his treatment nor he placed on record any original medical bill claiming medical expenses.

During his cross- examination, the petitioner (PW1) stated that he was working in State Bank of India as Manager and original medical bills have been deposited with the Bank and he had received 75% of the claim of medical expenses.
It is noteworthy that during enquiry proceedings, the petitioner did not place on record the detail of medical expenses remained unpaid from his department despite given several opportunities.
In the circumstances, I am not inclined to grant any compensation to the petitioner towards medical expenses.

20. Further, on perusal of the photocopies of the treatment papers, it is seen that he remained h o s p i t a l i z e d i n D e e p a k M e m o r i a l H o s p i t a l , D e l h i ,

sentences.text: He was diagnosed to have sustained 'inter- condylar fracture of right tibia' and during hospitalization, 'ORIF right tibia was done on 31.01.2017 under spinal anaesthesia'.
Petitioner also did not adduce any documentary evidence to claim the loss of leaves which he had to exhaust during treatment period.

Further, the evidence led by him did not suggest that he sustained any permanent disability on account of injuries and therefore, no claim for loss of post-retirement income, if any, due to disability arise here.

In the circumstances, considering the overall facts and circumstances of the case, more particularly the fact that the petitioner suffered grievous injury due to fracture of right tibia and he had to remain admitted in the hospital for about five days in hospital and during hospitalization, he had to undergo the procedure (ORIF) to treat his fracture of right tibia, it is quite apparent that he must have suffered immense pain and suffering during his treatment.

In these circumstances, I am of the opinion that the petitioner must be compensated with a reasonable amount for the pain and sufferings which he had to go through during his treatment as well as some amount towards special diet, conveyance and attendant charges which he might have incurred during treatment.
Hence, it would be just and fair to grant a lump sum amount of Rs.60,000/- to the petitioner as compensation.
Ordered accordingly.
INTEREST 21.
The petitioner shall also be entitled to interest @ 8% per annum on the compensation amount from the date of filing of DAR till realization.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is settled law that an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non
. However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.
Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v.
Himachal Road Transport Corporation & Others (2009) 13 SC 530, Parmeshwari v. Amirchand &
Others 2011 (1) SCR 1096 & Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. & Others 2018, Law Suit (SC) 303.
9.
In the instant matter, in order to prove his case, the petitioner, being injured as well as eye-witness of the accident, examined himself as PW1 and deposed on the strength of his affidavit Ex.PW1/A wherein he reiterated the facts as mentioned in the FIR and categorically deposed that respondent no.1 caused the accident, hitting him by the offending vehicle, being driven in rash and negligent manner.
Thus, in this scenario,
statemnet of R2W1 does not inspire confidence on the plea that he had not sent the respondent no.1 for delivery on the day of alleged accident.
Furthermore, the plea of false implication of the offending vehicle is also not sustainable in my considered view because no corroborative evidence in support of said contention has been placed on record by R2W1 i.e. the complaint to senior police officers or higher authorities regarding false implication or any previous enmity.
A conjoint reading of the testimony of the petitioner (PW1) and documents placed on record and exhibited by him as Ex.PW1/1 (colly) in the form of DAR which consist of FIR, Site Plan, Mechanical Inspection Report, Arrest Memo of driver/ respondent no.1, notice under section 133 of M.V. Act (having endorsement of owner/ respondent no.1 disclosing that respondent no.1 was driving the offending vehicle at the time of accident) clearly support the version of petitioner.
Thus, an adverse inference is liable to be drawn against him to the effect that the accident in question occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by him in view of the law laid down in case of Cholamandalam M.S. General Insurance Company Ltd. v.
Kamlesh, 2009(3) AD (Delhi) 310.
15.
As per settled law, compensation is not expected to be windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance A man is not compensated for the physical injury, he is compensated for the loss which he suffers as a result of that injury (Baker v.
Willoughby (1970) AC 467, page 492 per Lord Reid).
The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 ("the Act", for short) makes it clear that the award must be just, which means that compensation should, to the extent possible, fully and adequately restore the claimant to the position prior to the accident.
The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.
This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.
It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii), (b), (iii), (v)
and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
19.
In the instant case, the petitioner did not seek reimbursement of the medical expenses incurred in his treatment nor he placed on record any original medical bill claiming medical expenses.
In these circumstances, I am of the opinion that the petitioner must be compensated with a reasonable amount for the pain and sufferings which he had to go through during his treatment as well as some amount towards special diet, conveyance and attendant charges which he might have incurred during treatment.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Hence, it would be just and fair to grant a lump sum amount of Rs.60,000/- to the petitioner as compensation.
Ordered accordingly.
INTEREST 21.
The petitioner shall also be entitled to interest @ 8% per annum on the compensation amount from the date of filing of DAR till realization.
N o w , t h e q u e s t i o n a r i s e s a s t o w h i c h o f t h e r e s p o n d e n t s i s l i a b l e
. Admittedly, the offending vehicle was not insured at the time of accident and therefore, the respondent no.1 being driver of the offending vehicle is the principal tort feasor whereas, respondent no.2 being registered owner would have the vicarious liability.
Accordingly, the respondent nos. 1 and 2 shall be liable to pay the compensation amount to the petitioner and their liability would remain joint and several.
RELIEF:
23.
In view of above findings, this Tribunal awards a compensation of Rs.60,000/- (Rupees Sixty Thousand Only) to the petitioner/ injured along with interest @ 8% per annum from the date of filing of DAR till realization to be paid by the respondents.
The respondents are directed to deposit the award amount in A/c no.20780110171912 (IFSC Code:
UCBA0002078), UCO Bank, Karkardooma, Delhi, of PO MACT, Shahdara, through RTGS/ NEFT, within 30 days from today.
Respondents are also directed to give notice regarding deposit of the said amount to the petitioner and his counsel.
Disbursement of Award Amount :
24.
Manager, UCO Bank, Karkardooma, Delhi, is directed to release the entire award amount to the petitioner by way of transferring the same into his MACT Saving Bank Account after compliance of the award.
Direction to the Petitioner & his Bank 25.
The petitioner shall open a saving bank account near the the place of his resident.
Further, the bank of petitioner is directed to comply with the following conditions: -
(b) The original fixed deposit shall be retained by the bank in safe custody.
(d) The maturity amounts of the FDR(s) be credited by Electronic Clearing System (ECS) in the savings bank account of the claimant(s) near the place of their residence.
(e) No loan, advance, withdrawal or pre-mature discharge be allowed on the fixed deposits without permission of the Court.
(f) The concerned bank shall not issue any cheque book and/or debit card to claimant(s).
However, in case the debit card and/or cheque book have already been issued, bank shall cancel the same before the disbursement of the award amount.
The bank shall debit card(s) freeze the account of the claimant(s) so that no debit card be issued in respect of the account of the claimant(s) from any other branch of the bank.
(g) The bank shall make an endorsement on the passbook of the claimant(s) to the effect that no cheque book and/or debit card have been issued and shall not be issued without the permission of the Court and claimant(s) shall produce the passbook with the necessary endorsement before the Court on the next date fixed for compliance.
26.
With these observations, the claim petition is disposed of.
